"You cannot claim to 'think for yourself,' without being a skeptic. Skepticism is what keeps us as people from being led to the slaughter by those in power." - Anonymous

And that's why there's almost nothing that irritates me more than pseudoskepticism, and why it saddens me that pseudoskepticism is so common today.

I almost never, and most notably among self-proclaimed "skeptics" - encounter real skepticism. Real skepticism, when faced with an assertion that appears to be insufficiently supported, simply says, "Prove it." But most who pretend to "skepticism" in our overly rigid and narrow world today, when faced with an assertion that appears to be insufficiently supported, respond with "That's wrong," utterly failing to grasp the fact that that assertion is almost certainly at least as insufficiently supported.

Skeptics simply recognize and remain aware of unsupported beliefs and thus keep their minds able to adapt to any new information. Pseudoskeptics simply trade absolute and thus crippling faith in the nominal truth of an unsupported belief for absolute and thus crippling faith in the nominal falsity of an unsupported belief. Their minds are at least as rigid and blinkered and constrained - just in the opposite direction. And the most astonishing and discouraging part of it is that it's all too often people who wish to be seen to be notably intelligent - they're too smart to fall for whatever the belief is - but their own view is, if anything, even more simplistic and even less tenable than the belief they oppose. At least those who invest faith in the nominal truth of some unsupported belief have an actual viewpoint on something - there's some substance there, no matter the fact that it's unsupported. The pseudoskeptics view, on the other hand, is nothing more than the petulant child's "Is not!"

Yes - skepticism is, among other things, what keeps us as a people from being led to the slaughter by those in power. Psuedoskepticism, on the other hand, is what makes us deride those who break away from the herd.
A good line I heard once: "Modern Skeptics are just atheists with a fancier name". I wish I could remember the source.

I've heard it put very succinctly: "intelligent people question those who are in control, not those who question those who are in control".

"those who are in control" can be anybody: a teacher/professor, politician, parents, or simply anyone who claims to know more than you do about something.

However, keeping an open mind also implies having a willingness/preparation to admit when you're wrong. Lots of people skip that (crucial) step.

However, keeping an open mind also implies having a willingness/preparation to admit when you're wrong.

The common failure/refusal to do this is one of my biggest pet peeves, and I just ranted about it elsewhere the other day.

I understand that it's a challenge to ones ego to admit to being wrong about something, but in the first place, one should recognize that not admitting to being wrong actually does more to harm ones image than admitting to it ever could. It's pretty much guaranteed that there are going to be people out there who know for a fact that you're wrong, and then they're not only going to know that you're wrong, but that you're not even honest enough to admit it. So in the interests of protecting ones ego, admitting when one is wrong is the better alternative anyway - it causes less long-term harm. You can be wrong or you can be wrong AND a liar. The choice really seems pretty obvious.

Beyond that, and more importantly really, refusing to admit when one is wrong leads to clinging to views that are wrong. If one defends a view that one at least suspects is wrong, then one is likely to continue defending that view, and it's never going to get replaced with one that's even merely somewhat less wrong. And isn't the whole point that people want to believe that they're right? So isn't the best strategy to jettison every view that appears to be wrong as quickly as possible? If you want to be as right as you possibly can, clinging to views that you have reason to believe are wrong is a terrible strategy.

And there are even direct and measurable benefits to admitting when one is wrong. First and most directly, you generally actually get an image boost. Yes - some with an emotional investment in some notion of superiority are likely to crow about it, but most, without such an investment, are just going to be impressed to see someone being honest about it. You'll come to be seen as a person who's willing to admit to being wrong, which means that people are going to respect ones opinion that much more. And you're immediately free to rid yourself of that view and replace it with one that's at least somewhat more right, which means that your opinion is going to be just that much more accurate. So, in the long run, you'll not only be seen as a person who's more likely to be right about things, since it's been demonstrated that you'll admit when you're wrong, but you'll actually BE a person who's more likely to be right about things, since you've faced up to the times you were wrong and rid yourself of those views. It's a win/win, and the only thing standing in the way of doing it is the infantile squalling of ones ego.

And that's probably more than enough preaching for today....
